shows.title: Works on Paper, 2000-2018
shows.description: The gallery's sixth exhibition of the South African artist William Kentridge brings together prints and a drawing made between 2000 and 2018. The works use linocut, pigment print, drypoint, etching, lithography and charcoal, and many are printed onto pages torn from old books such as early editions of the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary and the Encyclopaedia Britannica, so each print is unique.

shows.title: Coherence in Chaos
shows.description: Seattle artist Michael Schultheis, who has shown with the gallery for 20 years, presents new paintings, pastels and bronze sculptures built around the epicycloid, the curve traced as one circle rolls around another. One center stands for a person finding inner balance, two for a relationship, many for families and communities, and the works ask what holds us together.

shows.title: Look Upon This Body As A Machine
shows.description:
Ilana Zweschi's second solo show at Foster/White pushes further into the strange territory where mathematics and figuration meet. Zweschi, who studied both art and math at Skidmore before an MFA in painting at SUNY Albany, builds her large abstract canvases from handwritten algorithms that dictate the placement and gradation of individual brushstrokes — but underneath that procedural surface sit figurative drawings, giving the algorithm an organic body to work against.

The results are paintings that read as abstract from a distance and only slowly reveal the ghosted figure buried in their logic — bodies rendered as systems, as the show's title bluntly states. Zweschi has shown at Tiger Strikes Asteroid in New York and in the Out of Sight survey of Pacific Northwest art, and her work sits in the Microsoft and SeaTac collections; this show marks a continued deepening of a practice that treats painting as equal parts intuition and equation.

shows.title: Shape|Shift
shows.artist: Jordan Hogan, Zoe Potter, Stella Bronson, and Cloe Short
shows.description:
Four recent Cornish College of the Arts sculpture graduates share SOIL's main gallery for a show built around distortion and the unspoken weight materials can carry. All four artists work with industrial castoffs — construction scrap, brick, steel, glass, latex — pressed into service to talk about bodies and femininity in ways that are anything but decorative.

Stella Bronson repurposes construction and recycled materials into large-scale sculpture that romanticizes the leftovers of rural labor; Zoe Potter combines glass, steel, latex, and hair into uneasy hybrid objects that push viewers back into an awareness of their own bodies. Jordan Hogan's sculptures fuse bricks and broken wood with worn stripper outfits, pairing two kinds of material history that are rarely allowed in the same room, while Cloe Short works with steel and concrete to probe the relationship between beauty and violence in the built environment.

Taken together, the show reads as a study in how industrial materials — usually coded masculine, structural, permanent — can be bent toward questions of gender, labor, and the body without softening into metaphor.

shows.title: Interchange
shows.description:
SOIL member Julia Monté's debut solo show in the gallery's backspace grew out of her childhood memories of Dallas during a period of explosive highway construction — stacked overpasses, scaffolding, and interchanges multiplying across a rapidly sprawling city. That early fascination with infrastructure has curdled, in her adult work, into something more critical: an interest in how these systems quietly organize and constrain daily life.

Working with repurposed material, Monté builds entropic, modular sculptures that echo the look of overpasses and scaffolds without literally reproducing them — structures that feel provisional, reclaimed, and slightly unstable, as if assembled from parts that used to serve some other, more solid purpose. The work sits somewhere between architectural model and ruin.

As a first solo outing, Interchange reads as a focused statement of purpose: reclaimed materials standing in for the systems, seen and unseen, that shape how people move through a city.

shows.title: As Seen In…
shows.description:
"As Seen In..." is J. Rinehart Gallery's chance to take a bow for a run of strong museum placements: it gathers gallery artists whose work has recently appeared in institutional shows around the country and puts that same work, or closely related pieces, on the gallery walls in Pioneer Square. Jaq Chartier, Katy Stone, and Emily Gherard all have pieces connected to "Women of the Pacific Northwest," a survey that traveled to the Bo Bartlett Center and the Asheville Art Museum; Cable Griffith's contribution relates to his Tacoma Art Museum exhibition "Uncanny Twilight"; and Priscilla Dobler Dzul shows work tied to her recent solo exhibition at the Frye Art Museum.

The result is a loosely thematic group show anchored by process-driven abstraction: Stone's layered cut-and-painted willow forms, Gherard's intaglio-and-plaster wall reliefs, Chartier's time-based chemical color studies, and Griffith's dyed and painted fabric compositions all approach observation and materials science from different angles, with an emphasis on unconventional or hybrid techniques.

It's a smart curatorial move — using museum validation as a lens for a commercial show — and a good one-stop introduction to several artists who've been quietly building serious institutional resumes without necessarily being household names yet in Seattle's gallery scene.

shows.title: Recent Work
shows.description:
Tucked into studio e's gallery annex, this focused presentation of new paintings by Bay Area artist Heather Wilcoxon runs alongside the main gallery's programming. Wilcoxon works from memory rather than observation, building canvases where strong, thick lines cut across colorful, atmospheric fields — a technique she's described as painting almost with her eyes closed, letting half-recognizable shapes surface from the subconscious.

The newer paintings on view continue the searching, oceanic quality of her longtime practice: forms that suggest familiar objects or bodies without ever fully resolving into them, so that looking becomes a kind of low-grade uncertainty rather than straightforward recognition. Wilcoxon has shown with studio e for over a decade, and this annex hang gives a compact, well-timed look at where her painting has moved since her last full show with the gallery.

It's a quieter complement to studio e's main-space program, worth a stop on its own for anyone who responds to moody, associative abstraction pitched somewhere between landscape and figure.

shows.title: Encore: Owls and Ravens – The Final Carvings
shows.description:
At 91, and after fifteen prior shows with Stonington Gallery, wood carver Hib Sabin is calling this one his last. The exhibition is built from his familiar bestiary — owls, ravens, shapeshifting guardians, small ritual vessels — carved from wood and often paired with the graphite studies that preceded them, so viewers can see a piece move from sketch to finished sculpture. Sabin has spent decades returning to the same handful of creatures as vehicles for thinking about aging, memory, and what gets carried forward, and that preoccupation feels especially direct here.

The carvings are small-scale and intimate rather than monumental, meant for close looking: weathered surfaces, deliberately worn textures, and animal faces that read as somewhere between totem and portrait. Because every major piece begins as a drawing, the show doubles as a look at Sabin's process, with works on paper offered alongside the sculptures they generated.

Billed as a final body of work rather than a retrospective, this is a chance to see a Pacific Northwest carving tradition — one Stonington has championed for years — brought to a deliberate close by one of its longtime practitioners. The opening falls on Pioneer Square's First Thursday art walk, with Sabin in attendance.

shows.title: In Celebration of Our 65th Anniversary: Masters of the Modern Northwest
shows.description:
Marking Woodside/Braseth's 65th year in business, this is a deep-bench survey of the painters who defined the mid-century "Northwest School" — Mark Tobey, Morris Graves, Guy Anderson, and Kenneth Callahan chief among them, joined by Paul Horiuchi's collage work and Louis Bunce. The gallery has pulled an unusually large run of works on paper alongside oils: Callahan's tempera and sumi-ink landscapes, Graves's tempera-on-gold bird studies, Tobey's ink and watercolor sketches of the old Pike Place Market, and Anderson's charcoal figure studies.

Because so much of the material is on paper and drawn from private holdings, this is a rarer chance to see the working, sketch-like side of artists usually represented by their signature large canvases — Tobey's small Pike Place Market studies from the early 1940s in particular offer a very different, more documentary view of the artist than his better-known abstract "white writing" paintings. Horiuchi's mixed-media collages, built from torn and layered paper, provide a textural counterpoint to the more painterly work around them.

Billed as being "in dialogue with" the mystically-inflected strain of Northwest painting these artists are known for, the show functions as much as a historical survey as a selling exhibition — a good primer for anyone trying to understand what critics meant by the "Northwest Mystics" label, and a chance to see significant works by these artists together in one gallery rather than scattered across museum collections.

shows.title: Everyday I'm Shuffling
shows.description:
Amara Eke returns to a body of work interrupted by the pandemic: an original 78-card tarot deck, begun as a senior thesis at Penn State, that reimagines the Thoth and Rider-Waite traditions with Black and queer figures at their center. The project is as much research as art-making — Eke dug into the history and visual conventions of tarot before deciding to rebuild its cast of characters from scratch.

The paintings and prints on view push back on how narrow and white the visual language of tarot and contemporary spirituality tends to be, recasting mystics, angels, and seekers as Black and queer protagonists rather than peripheral figures. Playful, galactic color and pattern-making keep the work from feeling didactic — it reads first as inventive design, with the representational stakes emerging on a second look.

shows.title: A Royal Flush in a Full House
shows.description:
Bonnie Hopper reimagines a deck of playing cards as a gallery of revolutionary and historical African Americans, rendered in an Art Nouveau idiom of flowing line and decorative pattern. Each portrait combines traditional oil painting with collage, African fabrics, mosaic tile, and resin, building up layered, tactile surfaces that ask to be looked at as closely as they were made.

Hopper, a Seattle-based artist, describes her practice as rooted in the tactile and the transformative, and the card-deck conceit gives the show a satisfying formal structure: fifty-two individually conceived portraits unified by a shared decorative language and a shared project of reframing overlooked figures as, in her words, a "safe port of call" where memory and craft meet.

shows.title: Between Us: An Afro-Diasporic Conversation With Seattle
shows.artist: Group exhibition, curated by Layomi Akinrinade
shows.description:
Curator Layomi Akinrinade gathers painting, photography, sculpture, film, design, and public writing around a single, open-ended question: what does it mean to make African and Afro-diasporic work in Seattle right now, approached not as a category to be represented but as a web of actual relationships to friends, venues, and institutions. Artists of other backgrounds are folded in too, reflecting the cross-cultural reality of the city's creative scene rather than a curated purity of identity.

Works on view range from Yolanda Galery's acrylic paintings to Nifemi Madarikan's metal-print photography, Ebony Luce's large-scale canvases, and Suneeva Saldanha's watercolor and ink drawings — a deliberately wide net that resists tidy categorization. The show is explicit about interrogating its own language, pushing back on how words like "diaspora," "healing," and "belonging" can flatten a work before it's had the chance to speak for itself.

CoCA has built the gallery into something closer to a social room than a conventional white cube, with seating and a visitor-response wall meant to encourage lingering and conversation, backed by a full slate of public programming including live music and a second First Thursday-style reception on September 3. It's a loose, generous show, more interested in real connection than thesis.

shows.title: The Mother Road: 100 Years of Route 66
shows.description:
Kellie Talbot paints the roadside vernacular of mid-century America — motel marquees, diner signage, gas-station lettering — rendered in oil with a close, almost forensic attention to rust, chipped paint, and decades of weather damage. This show marks the 100th anniversary of Route 66 with a full set of new paintings built around the highway's iconic neon signs, each one a small portrait of a specific business and a specific stretch of road between Chicago and Los Angeles.

Talbot has said she's drawn to these signs for the combination of color, rust, and typography, and that the wear visible in her paintings functions as a kind of memento mori for the roadside culture the highway created. The paintings range from tight close-ups of individual letters and bulbs to wider views that place a sign back into its motel-and-parking-lot context, and the show includes a mix of small-format studies and larger canvases.

It's a straightforwardly nostalgic subject handled with real technical control, and a good example of the kind of accessible, collector-friendly painting show Patricia Rovzar Gallery has built its reputation on over more than three decades in downtown Seattle. The opening reception doubled as a Q&A with the artist about the project's year of research and travel along the historic route.

shows.title: The Holy Purry Order
shows.description:
Carles Gomila's Seattle solo debut through Roq La Rue is a small, dense cabinet of oil-on-panel paintings built around a single, strange conceit: the cat as sphinx, familiar, and stand-in for the divine feminine. Working from Menorca, largely self-taught, Gomila paints in a lush, symbolist register that borrows the gilded, saintly framing of 19th-century devotional painting and the pulpy exoticism of mid-century illustration, then points all of it at the everyday intimacy between women and their cats.

Each panel restages a familiar art-historical type — a Madonna, a martyr, an idol — with a cat standing in for (or alongside) the female figure, so that reverence and camp sit uneasily together. Titles like "Our Lady of Terms and Conditions" and "Know Your Enemy" signal the show's wit, but the paintings themselves are sincere: richly glazed, framed like relics, and clearly made by someone who has spent real time looking at the psychology of cats as much as at painting history.

It's a tightly focused body of work — eighteen-by-twenty-four-inch panels in matching black-and-gold frames — and most of the pieces had already sold by the show's final week, which says something about how well this register of pop-surrealist devotion has landed with Roq La Rue's audience. Worth a look for anyone interested in the gallery's long-running lowbrow/pop-surrealist lane, and for anyone who has ever tried to reconcile loving a creature that mostly tolerates you.

shows.title: The World is On Fire
shows.description:
Sue Springer's installation turns the gallery into a small solar system of suspended ceramic globes, each one hand-built and surfaced with raised flame patterns, cartographic markings, and other textures that reward close, physical inspection. The spheres come in two sizes and are meant to be handled and rotated, so the piece functions less like a wall of discrete sculptures and more like an interactive constellation.

The subject is blunt by design: climate change and global instability, rendered through the recognizable shape of the globe itself. Titles like "Engulfed," "Ablaze," and "The Before Times" push the metaphor of a world under pressure without much subtlety, but the tactile, ceramic surfaces — each sphere different from the next — keep the work from feeling like a slogan. It's as much about the pleasure of surface and touch as it is about the anxiety of the subject matter.

Springer's use of clay, a material literally formed under heat and pressure, adds a quiet irony to a show about a planet doing the same on a much larger scale.

shows.title: Intention and Happenstance
shows.description:
Dodi Fredericks builds her mixed-media works on paper around a simple working method: a first gesture — a line, a brushstroke — followed by a response to whatever that mark does when it meets water, paper, and pigment. The results are large, fluid abstractions like "Convene" and "Crosscurrent," where washes of color pool and bleed at the edges of more deliberate marks, alongside smaller, more contained pieces such as "Migration."

The show's title gets at the push and pull in her process: how much of a finished piece is planned, and how much is the artist responding in real time to what the materials do on their own. Fredericks has cited Robert Motherwell's idea that a brush, left to its own devices, can find things a maker couldn't reach by intention alone, and that tension between control and accident is visible throughout the work here.

Alongside the exhibition, Fredericks is running a hands-on bookmaking workshop in the gallery, extending the show's interest in process into a participatory register — visitors can build their own simple sketchbooks using techniques she uses in her own studio practice.

shows.title: Tender
shows.description:
Kristin Tollefson, a Pacific Northwest sculptor known for public art and large-scale installation, fills METHOD's project space with a site-responsive work built from meticulous, hand-crafted forms that push against the gallery's own architecture. Trained as a metalsmith, Tollefson has spent her career working at the boundary between organic form and industrial material — wire, metal, and fiber worked with textile-like processes such as weaving and stitching — and Tender continues that line of inquiry at installation scale.

The piece leans into vulnerability and labor as explicit themes, using repetitive, handmade gestures to soften and complicate a hard architectural shell. It's less an object to look at than an environment to move through, in keeping with METHOD's mission as a volunteer-run space dedicated to installation work that "regards process, material, and concept" over discrete saleable pieces.

An artist talk with curator and educator Ellen Ito took place partway through the run, and the exhibition closes with a public activation — fitting for a show that treats its final form as something the audience helps complete.

shows.title: Edges of Unmaking
shows.description:
Daphne Minkoff paints Seattle's disappearing built environment — boarded-up houses, aging storefronts, abandoned cars — but this isn't straightforward documentary work. Her mixed-media collage paintings tear and layer old photographs into the physical structure of each piece, so the surface itself carries the same sense of accumulation and decay as the subjects depicted. Titles like "Dead End," "Vacancies," and "The Past Is Never Dead" point to the show's real subject: what persists in memory after a place is gone.

Many of the specific buildings Minkoff painted have already been demolished and replaced by condos and mixed-use development, which gives the work an odd double life — it's part elegy, part evidence. The largest canvas here, "Between Grief and Nothing" at 60 x 50 inches, anchors a group of smaller, more intimate collage-paintings that read almost like relics pulled from a demolition site.

Minkoff has been showing variations on this theme at Harris Harvey for years (an earlier iteration, Façades, covered similar ground), and this new body of work sharpens the focus on transformation and loss rather than just the buildings themselves. It's a quiet, materially rich show about what a city forgets when it rebuilds itself, and worth a slow look given how much is packed into the torn-paper surfaces.

shows.title: What's the Story? Contemporary Narratives of Home, Identity and Connection
shows.artist: Al-Baseer Holly, Eric Chan, Lauren Iida, Periko the Artist, Samantha Yun Wall, and Vincent Keele
shows.description:
Six Pacific Northwest artists use the human figure as a vehicle for personal and collective memory in this group show at ArtX Contemporary. Eric Chan's densely worked oil paintings on reclaimed wood braid together classical Western painting, Asian pictorial traditions, and queer and immigrant experience into a kind of invented folklore. Al-Baseer Holly builds his canvases from collaged photographs of himself and his family, fusing painting and personal archive. Lauren Iida's hand-cut paper works, built from washes of ink and negative space, extend her ongoing engagement with her family's Japanese American incarceration history into present-day social and political territory.

The show also includes Vincent Keele's saturated history paintings, which recover overlooked or invented figures from Black history, Gerardo Peña's (Periko the Artist) surreal, dissonance-charged scenes of migration and unbelonging, and drawings by Samantha Yun Wall, whose SAM Betty Bowen Award show is running concurrently across town. Read together, the works trade the single-artist survey for a chorus of first-person accounts of home, inheritance, and displacement.

It's a strong entry point into ArtX Contemporary's long-running focus on cross-cultural exchange, gathering artists working in wildly different materials — oil, cut paper, collage, graphite — around a shared interest in what it means to picture where you come from. A Story Time artist talk on September 12 brings several of the participating artists together in conversation.

shows.description:
Amanda Hood's new paintings work the seam between destruction and beauty — thunderstorms clearing to open sky, burned land pushing up new growth — as a stand-in for how people move through grief and transition. The pictures lean on contrast as their main tool: light against dark, clarity against ambiguity, sharply rendered passages set against passages left loose and unresolved.

Hood cites Susan Cain's writing on "bittersweetness" as a touchstone, and the paintings do carry that quality — heightened, elegiac, more interested in the emotional charge of a landscape than its topography. Paired with Uyen Tran-Gjerde's AWE + WONDER in CORE's gallery, the two solo shows form a contemplative, feeling-forward September program.

Shown alongside Amanda Hood's HEART MURMURS in CORE's shared gallery space, the two solo presentations make for a quiet, introspective pairing: both artists are working through personal material using color and surface as the primary emotional register rather than narrative or figuration. It's a modest, unhurried show worth a slow look rather than a quick pass-through.

shows.title: Self. Reflexive.
shows.artist: Ian Brownlee, Gegam Kacherian, Michael Lazarus, Kaoru Mansour
shows.description:
Self. Reflexive. gathers four painters and drawers whose work turns inward, using the figure and everyday objects as vessels for private experience. Ian Brownlee's large, autobiographical oil paintings stage specific memories — a birthday, a father's funeral — with just enough distance and symbolism that they read as shared human stories rather than diary entries. Kaoru Mansour's obsessively worked colored-pencil drawings on paper and wood panel push in the opposite direction, building tightly rendered, slightly uncanny psychological portraits out of pattern and repetition.

Gegam Kacherian's acrylic paintings supply the show's more abstract register: geometric fields and cosmic imagery (a recurring interest in his work since his years in Los Angeles) that read as maps of interior states rather than places. Michael Lazarus contributes a deadpan series of small, single-object paintings of chairs, each one a stand-in for a body or a mood, rendered with the flat clarity of a still life. Brownlee also built an interactive painting installation for the gallery's front room, inviting visitors to add their own narrative to the work on view.

Together the four practices make a loose argument that self-portraiture doesn't require a face — it can be a chair, a pattern, a swirl of color, or a remembered room. It's a quiet, drawing-and-painting-forward show, well suited to AMcE's intimate gallery space on Capitol Hill.

shows.title: I Have Eyes for You
shows.artist: Mary Anne Carter, Trisha Gilmore, Aimee Hagedorn, Sonja Peterson, Erika Rier, and Paige Wright
shows.description:
Running in AMcE's Niche Market storefront alongside the main gallery's Self. Reflexive., I Have Eyes for You is a playful, craft-forward group show built around a single motif: the eye. Mary Anne Carter, working with Wishbone Industrial Arts, contributes hand-cut and slumped glass tableware — plates, coasters, and trinket dishes — printed with eyes in a way that turns a dinner table into a small game of being watched. Other contributors work the same theme through embroidery, tufting, and ceramics, giving the show a lively mix of textures and materials rather than a single dominant medium.

The premise is light on its feet, closer to a design showcase than a gallery statement show, and it fits the storefront's function as AMcE's rotating venue for functional and wearable art. It's a good stop for anyone looking for a distinctive, handmade gift or object as much as for viewers interested in how far a simple visual joke — eyes on everything — can be stretched across different craft traditions.

shows.title: IN | ROTATION
shows.description:
Hannah Delaney's paintings for IN | ROTATION read like liner notes rendered as portraiture — a run of canvases built around the musicians who have stayed in her personal rotation as she moved from Atlanta to London and now Belltown. Rather than straightforward likenesses, the work leans on saturated color and flattened, poster-like composition to capture the feeling of a song more than the appearance of the person singing it, which keeps the paintings closer to concert-poster energy than fan art.

The show is split into two halves at Slip: the paintings proper, and a companion pop-up shop of posters, hand-painted jackets, bags, and other wearable work made by local women artists, with all proceeds returning to the makers. That pairing is very much in keeping with Slip's model as a community storefront gallery — the art and the marketplace share the same room rather than being kept separate.

It's a modest, high-energy show best experienced on a Belltown Art Walk night, when Delaney has also been doing live painting sessions alongside the exhibition.

shows.title: The Things We Call Things
shows.description:
Two Seattle-area artists who each came up through construction trades turn scrap material into sculpture in this two-person show. Bill Grader builds towers, stacks and wall-mounted assemblages from stained wood and painted scrap plastic — modular, brightly colored forms that read like architectural models built from salvage. Andy McConnell works in a similarly transformed vocabulary of found material, using scribing and carving techniques picked up on job sites to turn cast-off wood and steel into abstract, gestural pieces with titles like "Relic" and "Gradient Cycle."

What unites the two bodies of work is less a shared palette than a shared instinct: both artists treat construction debris — trim scraps, counter slab offcuts, blackened steel — as raw material with its own history, worth preserving rather than discarding. The result is a show about second lives for objects, built by two people who spent careers giving buildings their first ones.

It's a modest, unpretentious survey of outsider-adjacent sculpture that rewards a slow look at surface and joinery — the kind of show where knowing a maker's background changes how you read the work.

shows.title: Unwavering Hope: 18th Annual Juried Exhibit
shows.artist: John Affolter, Deb Choat, Jo Cosme, Elizabeth Costello, Claudia Kimberly Crayton, Whitney Diggs, Malialani Dullanty, Carol Eaton, Brooke Gassiot, Deirdre Herron, Amuri Morris, Gabriela Nirino, Jelisa Peterson, Gary Rubin, Randall Steinke, James Thatcher, Li Turner
shows.description:
Columbia City Gallery's annual juried exhibition returns for its 18th edition, this year built around the theme of hope as an active, sustained practice rather than a passive feeling. Jurors James Coley (King Street Station Program Lead, Seattle Office of Arts & Culture) and gallerist Avery Barnes selected the seventeen participating artists from a national pool of more than 350 submissions, so the show functions as a snapshot of how a wide swath of working artists are answering a shared prompt.

Given the loose, single-word premise, expect real range: portraiture that leans into quiet resolve or open laughter, textile and weaving work, and pattern-based pieces that use repetition as a stand-in for endurance. The curatorial framing — drawn from remarks by Auburn poet laureate Mateo Quispe about hope as "a matter of attention" — pushes the work toward political and personal registers at once, asking what it looks like to keep paying attention to what sustains us during hard stretches.

As a juried show rather than a single-artist presentation, this is less about a unified visual argument than about breadth: seventeen distinct voices circling one idea from very different angles, media, and life experience. It's a good entry point if you want a cross-section of what's being made across the country right now under one loosely shared theme, in the intimate storefront setting of this Columbia City co-op gallery.

shows.title: Fauna Aquatica: On Fluid Existence
shows.description: A group exhibition of eighteen artists, among them Tina Anderson, Julie Baer, Steve Jensen, Lezlie Jane, Tina Ostrander and Hanna Yudzina, looking at the creatures and landscapes of the ocean. The works range from painting and collage to textile and sculpture, picturing sea life as strange, beautiful and fragile. A printed catalog accompanies the show.

shows.title: Korean Rhapsody: Sijo at Gallery B612
shows.artist: MiYoung Margolis, KyoungMug Park, YoungHwa Choi
shows.description:
Three Korean-American artists build an exhibition around sijo, the concise three-line poetic form that dates to the late Goryeo Dynasty. Sijo's compressed structure — tension, expansion, resolution — becomes the curatorial logic here, with each work meant to echo that internal rhythm rather than illustrate a poem directly.

MiYoung Margolis, KyoungMug Park, and YoungHwa Choi work in ink, hanji (traditional Korean mulberry paper), and mixed media, translating calligraphic discipline and Korean literary tradition into a contemporary visual language. The show runs as a companion to a presentation the gallery staged during Korean Cultural Week at the Seattle Art Fair, and it's accompanied by live painting and dance performances and an ink brush workshop with Choi — a program that treats the exhibition as one part of a broader cultural exchange rather than a self-contained object show.

shows.title: I hear the hollow boom of time
shows.description:
Lotus L. Kang turns the Frye's galleries into a darkroom-scaled meditation on skin, memory, and chemical time. The centerpiece is a forest of raw, unfixed industrial film — sheets of the stuff photographers use to capture images — that Kang has exposed to changing light over weeks in a process she calls "tanning," so that the material itself develops a mottled, hide-like surface. Hung in cascading curtains and propped on tatami-mat bases, the sheets keep quietly changing for as long as they're on view, meaning the show is technically never finished and never quite the same twice.

A second gallery holds a kinetic sculpture built around a slowly rotating drum wrapped in celluloid, which throws moving bands of colored light across the walls in time with a score set to lines of poetry — an uncanny stand-in for a ribcage, breathing light instead of air. Works on paper made in dialogue with the museum's own architecture round out the installation, extending Kang's interest in translation, inheritance, and the porous line between a body and its environment.

This is Kang's largest museum presentation to date, and it rewards slow looking: the show includes a low-light room that can be disorienting, so give your eyes time to adjust. For anyone who knows Kang's photography-adjacent sculpture from biennials abroad, this is a rare chance to see it at full scale on the West Coast, and it's one of the most ambitious things on view in Seattle this fall.

shows.title: The Kondō Family: Storytellers in Clay

Their work grows from sometsuke, cobalt blue painted under a clear glaze, which each generation took in new directions, up to Takahiro's 'Silver Mist' glazes and cast self-portrait heads. Organized by SAM, the show is based on an exhibition first presented by the Lowe Art Museum, University of Miami.

shows.title: Discontinuity
shows.description:
French sculptor Gabrielle Wambaugh works almost entirely in stoneware and porcelain, but treats the material as something to obscure rather than showcase — her pieces are built through layering, concealment, and partial reveal, so that a form's full shape is never quite visible from any single angle. That approach carries directly into this show's title: "Discontinuity" gathers sculptures where surface, glaze, and structure seem to interrupt each other mid-thought, gold luster breaking across cracked or ruptured stoneware forms that look simultaneously ancient and freshly damaged.

Wambaugh's practice runs through some of the most serious ceramics research institutions in Europe, including multiple residencies at the European Ceramic Workcentre in the Netherlands and research time at the Sèvres national porcelain manufactory in France, and that technical depth shows in the way these pieces handle glaze as a kind of skin — fused, crazed, or gilded rather than simply applied.

This marks Wambaugh's exhibition debut at Traver Gallery's West Canal Yards space, and it's a good excuse to see the gallery's striking new home on the Ship Canal at the north edge of Queen Anne, in a former fish-processing building reworked into one of the city's more dramatic exhibition spaces.

shows.title: Light and Horizon
shows.description:
Marci Carlson's September show at Fogue turns entirely on the sky at its most dramatic hinge points — sunrise and sunset — rendered as a series of landscape studies gathered from locations around the world. The premise is simple and the execution is the point: how the same brief window of shifting light can transform an ordinary horizon line into something that reads as extraordinary, painting after painting.

As a single-artist survey built around one recurring subject, the show rewards being seen as a group rather than picking out individual pieces — the cumulative effect of repeated horizons in different palettes, from warm oranges and purples to cooler dawn tones, is where the work's argument about light and perception really lands. It's a straightforward, atmospheric show, well suited to Fogue's ongoing mission of spotlighting Pacific Northwest artists working past the emerging-artist stage of their careers.

shows.title: I Can See It From Here
shows.description:
Hank Reavis's solo show gathers paintings made between 2024 and 2026 that treat memory as an unstable, degraded signal rather than a fixed record. Working from personal photographs, Google Street View captures, and online archives, Reavis crops and pixelates his source imagery, then paints each pixel by hand — a laborious, almost perverse reversal of the instant, disposable nature of the digital images he starts with.

The result sits in a strange space between representation and abstraction: recognizable enough to read as places and moments, blocky and degraded enough to feel like something half-remembered rather than seen. It's a smart use of Mini Mart City Park's unusual venue, too — a reclaimed gas station turned art space in Georgetown, itself a monument to a site being reprocessed and given new meaning over time, not unlike the fragmented photographs Reavis reconstructs on canvas.

Rooted in Northwest painting traditions but clearly in dialogue with contemporary digital image culture, the show argues that memory's smallest, most degraded fragments can still carry outsized emotional weight. It's a compact, single-artist presentation worth catching during its short three-week run.

shows.title: Day-to-Day: Rhythm, Routine, Resistance
shows.description: A group show, mostly from the Henry's collection, about the poetics and politics of everyday life. Works from roughly the last thirty years by U.S.-based artists, among them Rashid Johnson's film of his family's routines, Dawn Clements' huge drawing of her temporary home and Tony Feher's hanging mass of plastic bottles, turn ordinary objects, rituals and rooms into places to think about labor, belonging and the forces that shape daily life. Artists include Nayland Blake, Andrea Bowers, Tara Donovan, Jenny Holzer, Louise Nevelson and Mickalene Thomas.

shows.title: Viewpoints: Shark by Richard Learoyd
shows.description: A one-work presentation in the Henry's Viewpoints series, which pairs a collection piece with responses from the University of Washington community. Richard Learoyd's Shark (2009) is a large, grainless unique print of a dead grey reef shark, made with a room-sized camera obscura he built himself. Writers from art history, anthropology and marine biology reflect on how it draws on scientific photography, still life and histories of extraction.

shows.title: Joiri Minaya: To Hell with Hibiscus
shows.description: New York-born, Dominican Republic-raised artist Joiri Minaya looks at 'the Tropics' as an invented place and identity. In the Henry's double-height gallery she shows the textile language she has built to critique it, from altered Aloha shirts to the floral spandex she designed to cloak colonial monuments, using Seattle as a link to shared histories across the Global South. The installation plays with hiding and revealing.

shows.title: screen-skin field: Seattle (Henry Art Gallery)
shows.description: A new mural for the Henry's exterior facade by New York artist Tishan Hsu, who since the 1980s has explored how technology shapes the body. Growing out of his recent wallpaper works, it blends skin-like textures, warped grids and grass-sprouting openings into a surface between the organic and the digital. Being outdoors, it can be seen any time.

shows.title: Charlene Liu: Scallion
shows.description: Eugene, Oregon artist Charlene Liu, born in Taiwan and raised in the Midwest, made the first mural for the Henry's Sculpture Court: a lush imagined landscape built from food-inspired forms. It continues her use of food to find culture and heritage in diaspora, celebrating shared meals and how culinary traditions build belonging. shows.title: Invention into Existence
shows.description: A large group show of nearly 20 artists and 30 works, including new commissions, on hopes and fears about technologies reshaping how we sense and live in the world. Its title comes from Frantz Fanon's call for 'introducing invention into existence', and it is arranged in three clusters: systems of knowledge, bodies as technological assemblages, and resource extraction. Many of the emerging and mid-career artists, including Morehshin Allahyari, American Artist, Stephanie Dinkins, Jes Fan and Tishan Hsu, are making their Pacific Northwest debut.

shows.title: The Henry Collection At 100
shows.description: For its centennial (it opened in 1927 as Washington's first public art museum), the Henry fills its original 1927 building with focused selections from a collection that has grown from 172 to nearly 30,000 works. Groupings look at representation, national myths, image economies, exchange between cultures, technology, and queer and feminist embodiment. Anchors include Winslow Homer's An Adirondack Lake (1870) with 19th-century landscape photographs, and Rauschenberg's Booster beside early video by Seattle's Doris Totten Chase.

shows.title: Amir H. Fallah: A Declaration
shows.description: The first commission in a new series for the Henry's three-story central stairwell. Los Angeles artist Amir H. Fallah, born in Tehran, will wrap the stairwell in a mural collaged from his archive of images and add sculptural tableaux with video collages in which people silently mouth 'I am an American', a portrait of American identity in its contradictions.

Lunacy is a set of intimate scenes in gouache, watercolor, acrylic, pastel and pencil about the cycles that shape a life, made as the artist entered perimenopause and lost a monthly rhythm, and about the guides, symbols and bodies met along the way. Supported by a 4Culture grant.
